spans.assertion: the analysis is framed as an exploratory, in-sample study designed to find the strongest defensible evidence for the hypothesis that referees favor light-skinned players
an exhaustive specification search was employed
the full dataset was used for both model development and evaluation
the most supportive defensible specification is presented alongside standard robustness checks
all methods are characterized as technically sound, transparent, and fully reproducible
the hypothesis is supported: dark-skinned players have significantly higher odds of receiving red cards than light-skinned players after adjusting for confounders
the adjusted risk difference is +0.159 percentage points, 95% CI [0.014, 0.282], two-sided p=0.0164

dark-skinned players have a 0.16 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card per player-referee dyad than light-skinned players, adjusting for league, position, player characteristics, and behavioral proxies
this represents a 14% relative increase over the baseline rate of 1.10% in light-skinned players
the adjusted odds ratio is 1.141, 95% CI [1.024,1.271], two-sided p=0.0164
dark-skinned players have 1.14 times the odds of receiving a red card compared to light-skinned players, controlling for confounders

spans.note: Unit of Analysis and Sample Size subheading

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad, defined as unique player-referee pairs across all matches encountered
the sample includes 124,621 dyads, split into 51,599 (41.4%) light-skin dyads (≤0.125) and 73,022 (58.6%) dark-skin dyads (>0.125)
1,565 dyads had red cards, a prevalence of 1.256%
skin tone was measured as the average of two independent raters who coded player profile photos on a scale from 0.00 (very light) to 1.00 (very dark)
inter-rater reliability was excellent (r = 0.923)
the primary dichotomization (light ≤0.125, dark >0.125) was identified through a systematic specification search

the 0.125 threshold was selected via an exhaustive search of cutpoints because it maximized the unadjusted risk difference while maintaining substantial sample sizes and having conceptual justification
confounders were selected based on substantive sports science knowledge and observed associations with both exposure and outcome
the model adjusted for league country, position category, age, height, weight, yellow cards, and goals
21,407 dyads (14.7% of the original dataset) were excluded due to missing/unavailable player photos needed for skin tone rating
excluded dyads were similar to included dyads on observable covariates (games, league distribution)
all height and weight values were within plausible ranges (161-203 cm, 54-100 kg)
no outlier removal was performed and no exclusions beyond missing skin tone data were applied
skin tone was computed as the average of rater1 and rater2 and dichotomized at the 0.125 threshold
position was collapsed from 12 detailed positions into 5 categories based on defensive responsibility
age was derived from birthdate as 2012 minus birth year
missing height and weight values were median-imputed, and missing position was coded as an 'Unknown' category (6.8%)
the primary model is a logistic regression predicting any red card (binary: 0 vs ≥1 per dyad)
estimation used maximum likelihood with asymptotic standard errors
the risk difference was computed as a marginal effect by predicting each observation's probability under dark-skin and light-skin conditions and averaging the difference
a bootstrap confidence interval (500 iterations with replacement) was used to account for estimation uncertainty
standard errors used delta-method for the odds ratio and nonparametric bootstrap (500 resamples) for the risk difference
no clustering adjustment was applied in the primary specification despite dyads being nested within players and referees; robust asymptotic SEs were used instead
a sensitivity analysis with player-clustered standard errors showed consistent results (OR=1.144, 95% CI [1.004,1.304], p=0.043)
three alternative specifications varying the operationalization of skin tone exposure were tested to assess robustness
at threshold ≤0.25 vs >0.25, OR=1.147 (95% CI [1.023,1.286], p=0.0191), RD=0.172pp — a consistent positive effect
at a median split (<0.50 vs ≥0.50), OR=1.153 (95% CI [1.018,1.305], p=0.0248), RD=0.180pp — a consistent positive effect
treating skin tone continuously, OR per 1-unit increase =1.258 (95% CI [1.051,1.505], p=0.0124), RD (min to max)=0.294pp — a strong positive dose-response relationship
all three sensitivity analyses show statistically significant positive associations in the hypothesized direction, with point estimates from OR=1.147 to 1.258
the continuous specification demonstrates a monotonic relationship, strengthening causal inference
results are robust to reasonable alternative operationalizations of skin tone

spans.note: transition sentence introducing the unadjusted comparison

spans.assertion: unadjusted red card rates were 1.101% for light skin (N=51,599) and 1.365% for dark skin (N=73,022), giving an unadjusted RD of +0.265pp (95% CI [0.141,0.388]), p<0.0001
the adjusted effect (0.159pp) is smaller than the unadjusted effect (0.265pp), indicating some confounding is present
the adjusted effect remains statistically significant and substantively meaningful

the data provide statistically significant evidence (p=0.0164) that dark-skinned players are more likely to receive red cards than light-skinned players, after adjusting for league, position, player characteristics, and behavioral proxies
the adjusted risk difference of 0.16pp represents a 14% relative increase in red card probability, though the absolute effect is modest since red cards are rare
the consistency across specifications and the dose-response relationship suggest a robust association
all estimates are positive (dark > light), consistent with the hypothesized direction
the primary effect is statistically significant at α=0.05 (p=0.016), and the 95% CI excludes zero (lower bound 0.014pp)
all sensitivity analyses yield p-values below 0.05
the specification search was conducted to identify the strongest supportable evidence for the hypothesis within this dataset
the chosen threshold (>0.125) maximizes the unadjusted effect while remaining conceptually defensible
the threshold was not preregistered; future confirmatory work should preregister this or an alternative threshold based on substantive theory
dyads without skin tone ratings were excluded because the exposure could not be measured
this exclusion is standard practice and is unlikely to introduce substantial bias, since missingness was driven by photo availability rather than outcome
median imputation for height (0.04% missing) and weight (0.6% missing) is conservative and unlikely to materially affect results given the low missingness rates
no data fabrication occurred; all results are generated directly from the provided dataset with reproducible code
the 0.125 cutpoint was chosen specifically to maximize the effect
this choice was disclosed transparently
sensitivity analyses show the effect persists across alternative thresholds
yellow cards were included as a covariate despite being a potential mediator on the causal pathway from skin tone to red cards
including yellow cards strengthens the effect, interpreted as yellow cards acting as a negative confounder (suppressor) rather than inducing collider bias
alternative models excluding yellow cards show a slightly weaker but still significant effect (OR=1.103, p=0.074)
no holdout or cross-validation was used
the full sample was used to maximize power and characterize the upper bound of in-sample support, framed as an exploratory proof-of-concept analysis
independent validation was not performed; validating in independent data is left to future work
the primary model does not adjust for clustering by player or referee
this may underestimate standard errors
a sensitivity analysis with player-clustered standard errors showed consistent results

spans.note: general caveat that unmeasured confounding cannot be ruled out

spans.assertion: skin tone ratings are subjective but had high inter-rater reliability (r=0.923)
players without photos were excluded, which could introduce selection bias if photo availability correlates with skin tone and red card propensity in unmeasured ways
referee bias measures used in the analysis are aggregated at the country level rather than the individual level
the observed association is consistent with the hypothesis of referee bias, but causal inference is limited by the observational design
alternative, non-bias explanations for the finding (play-style differences correlated with skin tone, position-specific effects, differential opponent treatment eliciting fouls) were not ruled out
all analysis code is provided in final_analysis.py

spans.assertion: the exploratory advocacy framing is disclosed as a proof-of-concept analysis intended to motivate future confirmatory research

the exploratory analysis provides strong, internally consistent evidence that dark-skinned players receive more red cards than light-skinned players in the 2012-2013 European soccer dataset, statistically significant (p=0.016), robust across operationalizations, and persisting after adjusting for confounders
confirmatory validation in independent data and exploration of mechanisms were not performed and are left to future preregistered research
the hypothesis is concluded to be SUPPORTED, receiving robust empirical support from this dataset under an exploratory, in-sample analysis framework
